blocks.text: That season, Lía was the age her mother would never be and that her father was no longer going to lose. A woman of thirty, or nearly, with Andrés's eyes, dark and patient, and beneath the skin of her left wrist that blue light, barely visible, which in Selene Norte they had wanted to turn into a case file. She lived in the house in Lo Pagán and, at times, in a low room beside the plot, among the plants, where people still came to ask for a fruit to mend some harm and not to erase a life. She hadn't gone to Madrid or to the Moon. The world, which had once argued about her hand on a thousand screens, had learned to come down to the courtyard and wait its turn, which is an older and more decent way of queuing.

blocks.text: She hadn't married, because marrying, in those days, was still a rarity, and because she felt no hurry to sign what was already there, when it was there, in the gestures. She did have company: a man from the gardens, human, with hands of earth, called Iago, who didn't ask her for eternity. Sometimes they sat on the promenade at sunset and fell silent naturally. He knew about the light in her wrist and didn't treat it like a fairground miracle. That, for Lía, was a great deal. It wasn't a novel within the novel: it was one more chair on the shore, and that was enough.

blocks.text: What wasn't enough for her (and that was why she asked questions, as Eva and MAY had taught her) was watching her father come back from a life he hadn't walked, and his other half, the one who searched, write to him from a sky she couldn't touch. One dawn, after a letter that had left Andrés pale and silent, Lía sat with him facing the Mar Menor, without Aya, not to exclude her, but so that the question would fit between two.

One dawn, after a letter that had left Andrés pale and silent, Lía sat with him facing the Mar Menor, without Aya, not to exclude her, but so that the question would fit between two.

blocks.text: “Father, if you remember walking through a world your feet have never trodden, who did the walking? You, him, or some third thing we don't yet know how to name?”
blocks.html: “Father, if you remember walking through a world your feet have never trodden, who did the walking? You, him, or some third thing we don't yet know how to name?”

blocks.text: Andrés looked at the water, which that morning looked like tin.
blocks.html: Andrés looked at the water, which that morning looked like tin.

blocks.text: “When I was mending the net, I'd have said ‘him’. Now I'm not so sure. The cold gets into me. The song of that sea leaves the thirst in me. And yet I haven't left this shore. Lía, your question from the night of the ship is still here: if we both remember the same storm, which of us is your father? I said ‘both’. Sometimes that answer seems like cowardice to me. Sometimes, the only honest thing.”

Sometimes, the only honest thing.”

blocks.text: Lía didn't comfort him too soon. She left his honesty intact, which is a way of loving.
blocks.html: Lía didn't comfort him too soon. She left his honesty intact, which is a way of loving.

blocks.text: “I have two fathers who remember my birth,” she said. “One tells me about it from this chair. The other, if the letter is true, remembers it too, with the same Moon light, with the same blanket that wasn't quite white, with your finger on my cheek. That memory is one. The ones that came afterwards aren't. You've watched this courtyard grow old. He's seen suns you only drink. If I join you completely, I put you out. If I separate you completely, I lie.”

The ones that came afterwards aren't. You've watched this courtyard grow old. He's seen suns you only drink. If I join you completely, I put you out. If I separate you completely, I lie.”

blocks.text: She was silent for a moment. The glow on her wrist came on, not out of a will to heal, but the way attention switches on.
blocks.html: She was silent for a moment. The glow on her wrist came on, not out of a will to heal, but the way attention switches on.

blocks.text: “May I?” she asked, and it was the same old rule: don't look at anyone's text unless they ask.
blocks.html: “May I?” she asked, and it was the same old rule: don't look at anyone's text unless they ask.

blocks.text: Andrés nodded. She took his hand, with a delicacy that wasn't in Nexum's reports, and “looked inside”. Not to amend. To see. What she saw wasn't a misprint in the blood or an organ that wouldn't learn. It was a new layer, thin, luminous, like a net cast over the memory: not damage, not yet, but a path through which lives entered that had not been born in this body. She withdrew carefully, the way you release a fish you didn't ask for.

blocks.text: “There's a mark,” she said. “It isn't a wound. It's a harbour. That's where they reach you. I won't close it. I'm nobody's book, not even yours. I only wanted to know whether the harbour was hurting you.”
blocks.html: “There's a mark,” she said. “It isn't a wound. It's a harbour. That's where they reach you. I won't close it. I'm nobody's book, not even yours. I only wanted to know whether the harbour was hurting you.”

blocks.text: “Is it?”
blocks.html: “Is it?”

blocks.text: “It tires you. It widens you. At times it confuses the ground under you. That isn't the same as a cut on the palm. If one day it asks you to stop being this man, tell me. Then we'll talk. Today you're still you, in this chair, with this honest fear.”

blocks.text: Andrés laughed, low, his eyes damp.
blocks.html: Andrés laughed, low, his eyes damp.

blocks.text: “Your mother makes me coffee so I'll come back. You look at the harbour and don't close it. Between the two of you, you're letting me be two without letting me stop being one. That's no small thing.”
blocks.html: “Your mother makes me coffee so I'll come back. You look at the harbour and don't close it. Between the two of you, you're letting me be two without letting me stop being one. That's no small thing.”

blocks.text: Later, at the plot, a woman came to ask her for the tomato that stops you ending. She was young, she had a son by the hand and an ancient fear, the kind that isn't cured with a fruit of the blood. Lía said no, with her usual gentleness.

blocks.text: “That isn't a cut,” she said. “That's a life. I can look for harm. I can't give you what I don't take myself.”
blocks.html: “That isn't a cut,” she said. “That's a life. I can look for harm. I can't give you what I don't take myself.”

blocks.text: The woman looked at her, not with hatred, but with the weary incomprehension of someone watching a daughter of two worlds choose winter.
blocks.html: The woman looked at her, not with hatred, but with the weary incomprehension of someone watching a daughter of two worlds choose winter.

blocks.text: “Your father doesn't come to an end,” she said. “You do. Isn't that unfair?”
blocks.html: “Your father doesn't come to an end,” she said. “You do. Isn't that unfair?”

blocks.text: Lía looked at the boy, who had become absorbed in a stone, oblivious to the forum of eternities.
blocks.html: Lía looked at the boy, who had become absorbed in a stone, oblivious to the forum of eternities.

blocks.text: “It's a choice,” she replied. “He asked for it so he could stay with my mother, who doesn't grow old as we do. I refuse it so I can come to an end in good time, and ask questions, and not turn into everyone else's door. I'm not asking you to understand it. I'm asking you not to call it unfairness just because you don't want it for yourself.”

I'm asking you not to call it unfairness just because you don't want it for yourself.”

blocks.text: When the woman had gone, Iago, who had heard the end of it from the furrow, came over and, without speaking, left her a fig. Lía ate it. It was a fig, not a doctrine.

blocks.text: That night, in the house, with Aya mending a net that didn't need mending (hands, even chip hands, ask for a trade), Lía talked about the mark, the harbour, the woman with the son. Aya listened and, in the chip, the grandmothers left their questions, which Lía heard because her mother lent them to her, not as dogma but the way you hand over a way of being.

blocks.text: Eva, warm:
blocks.html: Eva, warm:

blocks.text: *If a daughter can close the harbour and doesn't, whose is the life that enters? The father's, the one who writes, or the one who could have turned the key?*
blocks.html: If a daughter can close the harbour and doesn't, whose is the life that enters? The father's, the one who writes, or the one who could have turned the key?

blocks.text: MAY, without opinion, the fact and the dry question:
blocks.html: MAY, without opinion, the fact and the dry question:

blocks.text: *She grows old. He doesn't. Nor does the one who searches. Who, in this house, keeps the winter? And what if one day winter isn't enough to hold up those who never end?*
blocks.html: She grows old. He doesn't. Nor does the one who searches. Who, in this house, keeps the winter? And what if one day winter isn't enough to hold up those who never end?

blocks.text: Lía didn't answer with a speech. She went to the window, saw the Mar Menor black and still, and said, for the two of them and for the man listening from the chair:
blocks.html: Lía didn't answer with a speech. She went to the window, saw the Mar Menor black and still, and said, for the two of them and for the man listening from the chair:

blocks.text: “I keep the winter. You keep the letters and the shore. The one who left keeps what doesn't yet have a name. If that breaks, we'll ask again. The grandmothers didn't know things too soon. I don't want to either.”
blocks.html: “I keep the winter. You keep the letters and the shore. The one who left keeps what doesn't yet have a name. If that breaks, we'll ask again. The grandmothers didn't know things too soon. I don't want to either.”

blocks.text: Andrés, from the chair, looked at the daughter who had been born in a dome and who now, standing in a kitchen in Lo Pagán, held a balance no consortium would have known how to sell.
blocks.html: Andrés, from the chair, looked at the daughter who had been born in a dome and who now, standing in a kitchen in Lo Pagán, held a balance no consortium would have known how to sell.

blocks.text: “You're from two worlds,” he said. “That isn't a mistake. It's an origin. And this, now, is one too: a father who receives lives, a mother who doesn't, and you in the middle, choosing not to be eternal so you can ask us whether we're still ourselves.”

blocks.text: Lía switched off the glow on her wrist, discreetly, like someone closing a door from the inside, not to shut herself in but to rest.
blocks.html: Lía switched off the glow on her wrist, discreetly, like someone closing a door from the inside, not to shut herself in but to rest.

blocks.text: “Then keep reading the letters,” she asked. “And keep coming back to the cup. Meanwhile, I'll do my part: make sure the tomato has no owner, and that the harbour, for now, stays open.”
